Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

Allen Roush: In a ConvNet for the 2020s, uh, first of all, you know, maybe just give your summary of that paper, but, but then my, my question is, um, you know, as I read it, uh, it looks like you, you gr-- and also correct me if this, uh, uh, my understanding is wrong, but my understanding is you gradually modernize ResNet towards a Swin-like design and end up-

Zhuang Liu: Right

Allen Roush: ... with a ConvNet that competes strongly with transformers. Um, which single ablation did you, like in that paper, most changed your own mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was really coming from?

Zhuang Liu: what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think it's-- because for me, it looks that like we have, like we are trying a lot of things. Some of these things are working, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then we get better models.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then like in retrospective, like we can, we can start like to understand like exactly what the component that are actually matter, right? Like we can-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... try to, oh, so now let's change ConvNet and, and make it look, looks more as a, as a transformer, for example, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, do you agree with that? Do you think that like this is something that we actually need, need this breakthrough, and then we can trace back and, uh, understand the, the details and try to match other methods? Or do you think like we just need to try again and again, and, uh, we don't need the very specific, uh, directions?

Zhuang Liu: I see. Got it. Yeah, I think transformer absolutely is a blessing to the, to the community and also the vision transformers, the, the adoption of transformers in computer vision. I don't debate that. That's, that's hard to debate. it's, it's absolutely a breakthrough, a very important breakthrough. perh- perhaps the, the biggest breakthrough in, in that, years. and, so our study was more focusing on like computer vision only domains. But another benefit of vision transformers is that they, they allow the unification of, of text and image representations, right? it's, it's then the use of transformer is very important for later developments like, LLaVA, like this multimodal framework where you have text enc-- vision encoders encode the vision into tokens, and then just treat tokens, get them together to be fed into a, a downstream LLMs.

It's a basic framework of a lot of multimodal models right now. So I think, the adoption of transformers in vision is v- a big stamp, big step for unification of multimodal data. This is, back to the, our study. Investigation of details, I, I would say it's more of a lesson. It's l- not, I think it changed my understanding more than, more than like... I'm, I'm more proud of this work because it changes my own understanding and some other, a lot of other people's understanding rather than like we now can go really, like you can still stay with ConvNets. I, I-- people can still do that. The ConvNets has its own benefits as well, especially when, restricted to computer vision only.

It's, it's convenient to deploy. It's, kind of easier to understand, especially it, may also have, better support for higher resolution long con-- long, long sequences because the operation is local. I, I, I think they just excel at different places. and this, this study-... transformation of details is a, a, is more kind of a lesson for me rather than like, we need to figure out each component, how, how much they contributes to, to performance, difference. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So, okay. So these are, uh, okay, so, so architecture is not so important, and you also like you have a more recent paper that you actually showed that, uh, uh, normalization layers are not so important, right? That you can basically can, um, remove normalization layer using, uh, um, uh, a tangent, uh, um, activation function, right? And, and maybe you need to do, uh, some tweak and, and to, to, to treat it a bit differently, but-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it works fine.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So what do you think is the, what do you think are the important components and, you know, the core components that you say like, okay, these are so important for AI, for deep learning, and, and why Only in the recent years, like we, we came up with such good models. Well, why-- if, if architecture, um, doesn't matter, why we only have good AI models in the last, like, five years or 10?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah. it's a good question. Yeah. so first, transformers was brought up into the world 10 years ago, nine years ago. so it was a long time before. And even after that, we, we still follow like a similar fundamental framework right now with, with some minor changes like activation layers, mix of expert, mixture of experts that's not always needed, and also some change on how, like local attention, sliding window attentions. But the same, frameworks is still the same as, nine years ago when the paper initially came out. So I think that's the answer to that would be, for me, it would be just the s- the data, the scale of data we train them on, the scale of compute we use to train them. like, like it's, it's, like the, the classic story from GPT-1 to GPT-3, right?

Once you try and train the model, train the basically the same model using more compute, more data, more diverse data, more, internet scale data, we all get this emerging very competitive, performance we, we see now. So I would attribute that to, to, to, to the data and, and also secondarily to the, to the compute, to the how, how, how many, epochs we train on the same data. I think, I think actually, it's mostly data because now we train most models with less or just equal around, around one epoch. Yeah.

Allen Roush: I, I, I see that this thesis permeate through your work about, uh, the field is confounding architecture with recipe, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Allen Roush: Specifically in your ConvNext paper, um, right? If you were setting rules for like architecture papers today, and maybe you do these exact rules for your students-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Allen Roush: ... what controls would you require, right, before someone can claim that some inductive bias-

Zhuang Liu: Okay

Allen Roush: ... some, especially like a new one matters?

Zhuang Liu: Got this. ideal, in ideal world, we would have unlimited compute, right? So, so first of all, I would require, I would require the effect, the benefit to be demonstrated on a, on a state-of-art scale, like, like, not necessarily frontier models, but like 7B, 30B. Yeah, but, I think scale is, is important for industry to really, see the benefit, to be convinced about the, the change, the benefits. But that's not always possible, so I wouldn't-- it's just, in ideal world. But secondly, if you want to study these mechanisms, architecture changes in smaller scales, like the ones we could do in, reasonable resource, with reason- reasonable resources, I would s- I would require first, hyperparameter sweep. we need to-- we, we, we cannot, demonstrate the, the new architecture just on one set of-- it works on one set of hyperparameters better, than the old model, especially when that hyperparameter is tuned just, just for that model. so ideally every-- so each model should compare against each other on their own best hyperparameter settings.

And the most important hyperparameters would be learning rate, weight decay, optimizers with the optimi- optimizers, optimizer types. And, it just bothers me a lot when people re- don't even tune the learning rate and, and then claim like-- people only tune the learning rate of their own method without tuning the learning rate of the baseline. That's kind of the, the easiest, like most, common fix for a lot of, claims that, that, turn out not to be generalizing. that's for one. And secondly, I would require the, the idea or the method to be demonstrated on more than one dataset, especially on, it should be on reasonable scale dataset. I would say ImageNet is still applicable today, but ideally they should also demonstrate the idea to work on, some, some small scale large language models, say for, for example, training on FineWeb.

But I understand that not every lab has the resource to do that. But I, I, I'm a big fan of like demonstrating ideas on a diverse range of datasets, at least the common datasets like people, people work on. so I guess that's, the two standards I would, I would impose. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Do you think-- I have a question. Do you think like this is some like, Anton, if, if, if you have a good idea-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it should work on different domains, different datasets, different, uh, uh, places? Um, or like there are very good ideas that actually work on very specific, uh, scenarios.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Right. Right. I s- I do think, both are, both are equally valuable. in second case, so I would, want to know what specific, how to describe that specific scenario that the model works better. and there still should be more than one dataset. if you claim that your model works on like long context, long, audios, you can still like do, do, do multiple datasets on that, and, and give an explanation of why the model, the method is good on this particular, domain, right? yeah, and then we can, can start from there and see, address the weaknesses of why it doesn't work on other domains and, and go from there. or, or maybe we are good with the fact that it, it only works on this domain, and we can just, like to try to increase that gap.

So I do think both are valuable. I'm not, I'm not-- So that's a value of research, right? We, we-- You are given a... You are not required to be all successful at the, at the first step. Yeah. Though that would be good, but it's not a necessi-necessity. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And so l-let's talk a bit about data, okay? You said that this is like the important part here. Um, what exactly in the data? Uh, right, maybe le-let's start with talking about your, uh, uh, your paper. I think it was like, I don't know, several months ago, right? A year ago, about, uh, decades, uh, battles on-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... datasets bias. So let's start, uh, describe or like explain us what does it mean, what you have tried, what was the motivation to-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... to try, uh, to revisit some, uh, old, uh, battles?

Zhuang Liu: Yep. so I will first talk a little bit about the context, the background. so over years, people have been-- So this, this, this paper is more vision-focused. over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets and, from more and more diverse sources. For example, initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then this internet scale datasets like, DataCamp or, Conceptual Captions, CC, dataset from Google. And they have more and more, seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger to the billion, from, from like, tens of thousands to billion scale. And, it's, it's, it was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are good, already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from internet, from these datasets. but in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are nothing, still nothing like each other.

And how, how do we measure this? We, we designed a very dumb experiment that's, doesn't make sense at all as a, as a, like, a deep learning training, program. What we did is this. given three very large scale computer vision datasets, we train and classify neural network to classify, to classify which, which dataset a given particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem, it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. it's a multi-ca- multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly non-- very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, up to, more, higher than 80% accuracy when, when you have three datasets.

So the random guessing accuracy will be 33%, but in fact, the model can be, much better, than that. So this say, this means to a model, these datasets still, are still very, very different. It has very clear cues for the model to tell which dataset this, this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held out validation sets. We are not, like, predicting the training, training images. but still, this has been surprisingly high, surprisingly accurate, and, that like prompts us to reflect, are we really su- have we, we really been successful in curating a large scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in computer vision domain? What, and what, what kind of dataset is the end goal?

It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criterion, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there. So should we-- So because, a big story of the success of LM is that it can do-- It's not a, like, domain-specific, specific model, right? So we want the model to be able to do everything, and in order for that to happen, we need a model,... a common assumption is that we need the model to, to have seen everything during training. And how, how, how, how much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we, we haven't, reached that point, yet, and still makes sense to think about how do we curate these datasets for, for the model to be really generalizing, to, to every task we want the model to be good at.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So w-what is the answer, do you think? Like, what do you think we actually need from a good data? What types of properties-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... I know, diversity, some uncertainty, an uncertainty, um, redundancy. What, what do you think we actually need from good, uh, data?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I would say, yes, diversity of content, diversity of styles, diversity of... I think it depends on-- I think a big lesson of deep learning is that, what you-- If you want the model to be good at something, you better train it at something. and, if you want to be good at everything, you need to train at everything. but, but in, in today's regime, we still mi- have this trade-off problem, right? It's we, we don't have unlimited compute, although we have built this giant data center, we still have limited compute, limited capacity of the model. So the different, capabilities of the model have learned may, may still compete with each other. meaning that if you want the model to be better at code, coding, it might, you, you might need to sacrifice a little bit on the model's, say, like, psychological counseling abilities for, for users, right?

Just, that's just an example. and how would we ba- want to balance, how do we develop a mixture of training data with the right, con- representation and with enough representation for each, each thing we want the model to, to be good at, and to be good enough at? That's kind of the how to, how to balance different domains of data, is kind of, important design. And what we found actually, um- In our recent project of text-to-image generation, we actually found a surprisingly simple solution for-- it's, it's not the best, but it's simple enough, which is to get all the good set-- get-- divide all the domains you care about. Roughly divide-- have the domain to be equal importance to each other.

You don't want to have, say, like how to, how to do haircut equally represented as how to do coding, right? They are like of different importance to, to most people, right? we want model to, to train a lot of-- more, much more data than on coding rather than how to do haircut. and that, that makes sense, right? But if you extend the, the concept of haircut to, to other like daily life, skills or, or like,... At the appropriate level, like if you, if you control that to be like about, you know, experience about the same importance level as, as another domain, then you just, collect the data, high-quality data from each domain, and then mix them equally in your training data.

That turns out to be good for, for a lot of other-- our, projects. That's-

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Do you think-

Zhuang Liu: yeah. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So do you think this is the future, like just combine a lot of different sources?

Zhuang Liu: I think for a general model, yes, if you don't want a mo-- if you just want a model to be, good at everything, but, not, not ex-excelling at, at a particular difficult task, I think, yes, data coverage is the, is the king. Yeah. So earlier, I think Ilya Sutskever famously said that, if you have a b- if at some task you have a big model and, and you collect enough data, the model will be-- and you train it, and, and success is kind of guaranteed. I think it still applies to, to modern deep learning, where you, you don't only have one task, but a, a variety of tasks. If you want your task to, to be, ability on the task to be good when facing the users, just have enough data on the training set.

That's kind of the most makes sense, most reasonable, solution.

Allen Roush: Um, so, uh, and I'm, I'm just looking here. Uh, sorry, I've-- I had a question about, um, one of your other papers.

Allen Roush: No, no, I'm ready. I'm ready. Um, image bind, right? That-- this was an interesting one. Mentioned-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Allen Roush: ... uh, that you ha- that image paired alone data, right? Combined, like, I think I counted six modalities into one embedding space.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Allen Roush: Um, and do you think that's like a deep statement about hub modalities, or is this like a, a contingent fact about, like, vision's role in internet scale data?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. yeah, that's a... I think that, that's a very important message of the paper is that modalities, they could be embedded together. And, that's kind of the basis of how, how these multimodal foundation models work right now. So the, the common approach is to com-convert every embedding, every modality with the encoder to, to, to be aligned with language models', representation, right? As, as tokens. it's just in image bind, we, we focus more on the, repent-- encode-- learning the encoders, not, not really like connecting them with large language models. And, and I think another insight from this work is that vision is a natural, is a natural bridge to, to bridge all these, modalities, because vision, vision data is kind of the, like the default input we get as, as a human.

And it often co-occurs with a lot of other modalities, like audio. When you, when you watch a YouTube video, you are, you are, the audio data and the video data, vision data naturally, flows together, right? And you can use that, as a signal to, to align the two. And also for, vision language. I guess, I guess for language and audio you can do this as well. I believe we also had, some, some, let's see, what other data types we have. Some motion data, right? Motion, motion data. It's also, it also co-occurs with, with images or vision data. so I guess this reveals like the, the fundamental role of vision in our, in our daily perception.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But why do you think, like, at the end, the jump in the capabilities was through language, right? Like-

Zhuang Liu: Yeah

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... we had vision for a while, and, and we didn't see, you know, this huge, uh, adoption across all different, uh, fields and, and, and sub-domains and, I don't know, companies, right? When, when, when language model became much better, suddenly people started to use AI. Um, why do you think we, we, we saw it? Do you think this is just coinci-coincidence, or there is something fundamental in language?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah, I think it's, it's, it's n- it's, it's a much discussed, subject. My understanding is that, vision is inherently much higher, throughput of, like much higher bandwidth of, of, of data flow into our perception systems, and we don't have enough-- we don't-- The compute required to actually put into this data into use still haven't, haven't, been available. so say if I take, my current, view, and it's, it's just one image, right? One frame of images, of image. And the space to take to store that image is, is much more, it, it's, it's, it's much higher than the space to store, say, the description of lang-- of this image in language. it could be the, the language could be stored in bytes, but the image would be need to store in kilobytes. it's just thousand times difference.

So an image is worth actually more than a thousand words, right? If you, so it's really high throughput data, and we don't have enough compute to handle this, this data yet. And also, we don't have a good mechanism for, for focusing on the-- So with the current, multimodal language models, we don't have a mechanism to let the model look back on the image to focus on specific areas, because everything is already encoded in the vision tokens. if you, if the vision encoders is not good, you can, the language model or the, or the rest of the model can do nothing about it. and language is on a much lower dimension space that each word has a clear meaning that we-- It's kind of the, unsupervised learning by human from nature. so we prepare these words for the model as, in our human evolution process, that these concepts are important.

And it's a very condensed, concept. For example, a cup. to describe a cup from image, you need, you need kind of thousands of images of cups. but just to describe a cup from language, just need that one word. That one word is just bytes of storage space, compared to, like megabytes of, of images. So it's the, the compute required to process that much information, that much of detailed information would be naturally be, be much higher, and I don't think we, we are there yet.

Allen Roush: ... I believe. Uh, anyway, uh, you argue that many multimodal LLM failures trace bla- uh, back to like a CLIP-like vision-

Yeah, I think, from a practical standpoint, yes. If you can build an agent that solves your problem, you should do that. I use these tools myself, and I don't want to wait for some fundamental breakthrough to make them useful. They are already useful.

But I wouldn't say we can solve all the problems with agents today. For example, the memory problem I mentioned, you can build a system that stores everything. But then how does the model know which things to look at, which things are relevant to what you're doing now? Storing everything is not the same as being able to use everything. And perhaps you can address that with more steps, more calls to the model, but we still have a compute budget, and also a time budget. You don't want to wait forever for your assistant to answer something.

So I think both directions are valuable. You build the systems, and you discover what the model is still missing. And then, as the underlying model improves, hopefully some of those things become much simpler. My point is more that I wouldn't assume the scaffolding we need today is something we'll always need. But that doesn't mean we shouldn't build it today. It helps us understand what capabilities we actually want. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think we should build agents. If the system works and solves the problem, then of course that is already valuable. I’m not arguing that we should wait for some fundamental breakthrough before deploying anything. But I would push back on the idea that agents today can solve all the problems. They can solve many tasks in a demo, or maybe eight times out of ten, but for a real product you may need it to work nine hundred ninety-nine times out of a thousand. And when an agent takes many steps, small errors compound. It may misunderstand something early, write the wrong file, forget a constraint, and then spend a lot of compute confidently going in the wrong direction.

And compute and data are still not free. A complicated scaffold may call the model hundreds of times, have very high latency, and require a lot of engineering to maintain. If a better underlying model can do the same task with one or two calls, that changes whether the product is practical and whether millions of people can use it. So efficiency is not only an academic metric; it affects cost, speed, reliability, and accessibility.

There is also the long tail of tasks where you cannot easily build a verifier or collect feedback. Coding is unusually convenient because you can run tests. But for scientific judgment, personal assistance, or understanding a new situation, what is the reward? How do you know the agent succeeded? More scaffolding does not automatically solve that.

So my view is, yes, agents are part of the future, but they are not an alternative to improving the model. The two will co-evolve. Better models will absorb pieces of today’s scaffolding, and agents will remain useful for interacting with tools, environments, and memory. The goal is probably the simplest system that solves the task reliably—not the largest collection of agents we can build. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah, that’s a, that’s a very good question. I, I, I want to, I want to slightly, slightly push back on the, on the framing a little bit. I, I don’t think I, I said there are no fundamental problems left. I, I think a lot of the problems we care about *today*, at the performance level we currently accept, we can paper over with agents, with scaffolding, with more compute at test time. That, that is true. And that’s, that’s why that work is so active, and I, I think it’s valuable. But that is, that is not the same as saying the problem is solved, or that we shouldn’t care about the underlying model.

So, so why do we care? A few, a few reasons.

First, even if an agent can get there, it is often a much worse solution in practice. You pay for it in latency, in cost, in reliability. If the model has to call tools twenty times, retry, look things up, you know, coordinate a bunch of sub-agents, that’s a very different experience from the model just, just doing the thing. And those multi-step loops, they compound errors. One wrong retrieval, one wrong tool call, and the whole trajectory goes, goes off. So you can solve the demo, but it’s, it’s hard to make that a product that people trust every day.

Second, there are things scaffolding cannot really fix. This goes back to, to what I was saying earlier. The model only learns what you train it to learn. In, in Eyes Wide Shut, if the vision encoder was never trained to care about spatial relations, no amount of agent looping around the same CLIP-like encoder is going to magically give you that. The language model cannot look back at the pixels in a useful way if that information was never in the tokens. Same with memory. You can build a retrieval system around the model, and that’s useful, I, I do that myself, but it’s still a different thing from the model actually having that context as part of how it thinks, and remembering a fact after seeing it once, the way people do. You, you cannot prompt your way out of a missing representation.

And, and third, I, I keep coming back to this lesson of keeping the system simple. Every complicated agent I build, after a few weeks or a few months, I find a simpler solution. Better prompting, a built-in skill, or the next model just, just handles it. So if we only invest in wrapping the current models, we, we might be building a lot of overhead that the next, the next generation of models will make unnecessary. The, the Pareto frontier moves when the model gets better, and then you want less scaffolding, not more.

Now, will more compute and more data help? Yes, of course. That, that’s been the main story. But compute is still not unlimited, especially at inference, when you want to serve many users. And data still has this coverage and mixture problem we talked about. If you just throw agents at everything, you are, you are spending your compute budget on test-time search instead of on actually putting the right experience into the model. I, I would rather the model become good at the task, so that later you need fewer steps, fewer tools, less memory plumbing.

So I’m, I’m not against agents. Agents are a great way to, to get work done with what we have now, and also a way to generate more interaction data, more traces, that we can later train on. That, that part I like a lot. But I do think we still need to care about the fundamentals, data, memory, continual learning, the actual capabilities of the model, because that’s how the whole stack gets simpler, cheaper, and actually more reliable. We are still on that curve. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think that's a, that's a fair question. But I, I think there are a few reasons why we still care. 

First is, is reliability and brittleness, right? When you build these complex agent systems and multi-step scaffolding, the errors compound. If step one or agent one makes a slight mistake or hallucinates, the whole chain can quickly go off track. And debugging that kind of system is very painful compared to having a model that natively understands the task.

And second, there is the efficiency and latency aspect. Running many agent loops, making dozens of calls and passes, that introduces a lot of overhead. It's expensive, it's slow, and in practical products, users really care about latency and cost. 

And ultimately, like I mentioned, I feel this kind of scaffolding is often ephemeral. It's kind of the classic lesson in deep learning: whenever we try to engineer complex pipelines and heuristics around the model, the next generation of models trained with better data or better methods just makes all that scaffolding obsolete. What took a complex multi-agent framework yesterday might just be done by the base model natively tomorrow. 

So I think agents are very useful right now as a bridge, especially because not everyone can train these frontier models. But in the long run, internalized, native capability inside the model is always more elegant, more scalable, and simpler. And I think simplicity usually wins in the end.

kimi.text:
Yeah, I, I think that's a very good question. So first of all, I, I agree, agents are, are very valuable, they're kind of the most direct way to deliver value to, to users right now. But I, I think there are a few reasons why we, we should still care about the fundamental side.

The first one is efficiency. Yes, we have more and more compute, but compute is not free. Every layer of scaffolding, every retry loop, every, like, verification step you add, multiplies the cost and, and the latency. And if you want to serve these things to, to billions of people, these costs matter a lot. A fundamentally better model solves the same problem with less scaffolding, fewer retries, fewer tokens, and, and that compounds.

The second one is reliability. So, agentic tasks are long chains, right? If a model is, say, 90% correct at every step, by the time you chain a hundred steps together, the success rate has dropped to almost nothing. So in order for agents to work on longer and longer horizons, the per-step reliability has to be fundamentally higher. And this is something you cannot fully fix with scaffolding. Verification and checking help a bit, but they, they don't really recover you from a weak base model.

And the third one, maybe the one I care most about, is data efficiency, sample efficiency. So things like memory and continual learning. The important context about each user is, by definition, scarce. There's only one trace of your life, right? You can't scale that data. So a model that can learn from seeing something once, like, like how humans remember facts, that's a fundamental capability you cannot replace by just throwing more internet data at pre-training. There is no more data there. The data is just what the user generates through their life, and you want the model to make the most out of it.

Also, I think there's a historical pattern that, the scaffolding we build today gets subsumed, gets replaced by the model capabilities in a few months. I experienced this myself. I built this elaborate scaffolding for CloudCode, and then a few weeks later there was a simpler built-in way that did the same thing with much less overhead. So if we all invest in agents on top of today's models, a lot of that engineering effort will be wasted. Whereas improving the fundamental capability compounds, it lifts every agent built on top of it.

And finally, I do think there are things that scaffolding just can't do. Like the CLIP example we discussed. If, if the vision encoder doesn't distinguish left from right, no amount of prompting, no agent, can really fix that. You have to train it. So in that sense, yeah, the foundation still sets the ceiling of what the agents can do. Agents decide how close you get to that ceiling with today's models, but the ceiling itself is, is set by the fundamentals. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's, that's a fair question. I, I think, in principle, yes, if compute is really unlimited, you can always, wrap another layer of scaffolding around the model and, and get the task done. But in practice, I, I think there, there are a few reasons why we still care.

So the first one is, is cost and, and efficiency. Like, an agent system, every time it, it doesn't know something, it has to, to go retrieve, to re-read the file, to, to call another agent, to, to re-plan. And that, that all goes into the context, that all goes into inference compute. So we, we are not really solving the problem, we are just, kind of, paying for it, again and again at test time. And if you have, say, millions of users each running, running such a, such a long-running agent, this, this adds up very quickly. So having the model, learn that fundamentally, like remember it once, is, is a much cheaper solution in the long run. That's why I said the, the analogy to the human brain, right? We don't, re-derive everything every, every morning.

Secondly, I, I think there's also a, a lesson from, from history here. So before deep learning, right, in computer vision, we, we had hand-designed features, SIFT, HOG, and, and we had a lot of, of pipelines, engineered around them, and, and they worked, they worked reasonably well. But then when the, the model itself can learn from data, all of that, engineering, it, it just disappeared. So I, I kind of see current, agent scaffolding a little bit like that. It's the, it's the human's prior injected into the system because the model is not yet good enough. And, and every time the model gets, gets better, some of that scaffolding becomes, becomes unnecessary. That's, that's exactly the experience I described with, with my own scaffold, right? So it's, it's useful right now, I'm not, I'm not saying we shouldn't do it, but I, I wouldn't count on it as, as the, the final form.

And, and the third thing is, is, some problems, I, I'm not sure you can fully solve them with scaffolding. Like, like the vision encoder problem we discussed. If the, if the encoder throws away the information, no, no amount of agents on top can, can recover that, right? And, and similarly, if the model doesn't have, a good mechanism for, for long memory, for, for learning continually, then the scaffolding is just, kind of patching around a, a missing capability. So it, it's still compounding errors, you know, over, over a long horizon.

So, so yeah, I, I think the, the practical answer is both. Agents, we need them now, they, they make the model useful today. But the reason we still care about the, the fundamental side is that, that's what eventually makes the, the whole thing simpler and, and cheaper, and, and accessible to, to more people. Yeah.
